clue.text: Be proud about boy and girl not finishing rejoicing

indicators.note: the word about means one piece goes around the other pieces here

parts.note: to be proud is to jut out, stick out from a surface

indicators.note: the boy and girl are both not finishing, so each name loses its last letter

parts.note: Bill is a boy's name
Ann is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone is told to take pride in a young couple who keep stopping mid-word in their celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finishing' cuts the last letter from BILL and from ANN, leaving BIL and AN, which JUT goes 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jubilant and rejoicing are synonyms, both meaning triumphantly joyful.

clue.text: See 3
Musicians defining council tax?

explanation.surface: A group of players is asked whether they set the local property levy.
explanation.walkthrough: UK council tax is charged by valuation band, A to H, so a band is what defines the amount a home pays.
explanation.definitionFit: A band is a group of musicians, and also a property valuation bracket fixing British council tax.

clue.text: Set fire (a short story) to flag and call sailors with glossy fruit eaten by Queens' fellow having Christmas dinner?

parts.note: lit means set fire to, ignited

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so the story is short of the letter a

parts.note: a tale is a story
the letter a, as written
a jack is a small flag flown at a ship's bow
ho is a call, as in land ho
RN is the Royal Navy, hence sailors
ER is the Queen (Elizabeth Regina); the plural Queens' supplies two of them
satin is a glossy finish, as in satin paint
an acorn is the fruit of the oak, the kind eaten by pigs; eaten by just leads on to the queen
the second queen from the plural, again ER for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A rambling instruction mixing arson, flags, sailors and a college fellow at the festive table.
explanation.walkthrough: Araucaria's long clue is loose: the plural 'Queens'' supplies the queen twice, and 'eaten by' only links. Little Jack Horner sat in a corner eating his Christmas pie.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme Jack Horner sits in a corner eating Christmas pie, so he is a fellow at Christmas dinner.

clue.text: Adoptive, perhaps, without extra enzymes?

explanation.surface: Adopted parents are likened to a washing powder free of added enzymes.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-bio washing detergent is a British product sold without the enzymes of biological powders.
explanation.definitionFit: An adoptive parent is not a biological one; a non-bio detergent has no added enzymes.

clue.text: See 3
Love would vex the devil

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O
'ld is the old contracted form of would, as in Shakespeare's you'ld
to harry is to harass or vex

explanation.surface: Romance would only annoy the devil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ld is an archaic contraction of would, seen in older texts as you'ld or I'ld.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Harry is a traditional nickname for Satan.

clue.text: Inattention to information arising: vermin have suppressed it

indicators.note: in a down clue, arising means the word reads upwards, so backwards

parts.note: gen is slang for information

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down within, so the vermin enclose it

parts.note: lice are vermin
it refers back to the information, so gen again

explanation.surface: Someone ignores news cropping up about a pest infestation that has been hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arising' turns the slang word for information upwards; 'it' then stands for that same information, which 'have suppressed' tucks inside the vermin.
explanation.definitionFit: Negligence is a failure to pay proper attention, so it means inattention.

clue.text: Polite and calm without some peculiarities

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the calm word goes around the rest

parts.note: restful means calm, peaceful

indicators.note: some of signals that only part of the next word is used, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Being courteous and serene, free of odd quirks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking: the calm word wraps a run taken by 'some' from 'peculiarities'.
explanation.definitionFit: Respectful behaviour shows deference, so it is polite.

clue.text: The Lady of the Lake?

parts.note: not the Arthurian figure but a woman's name shared with a big lake on the German, Swiss and Austrian border

explanation.surface: An apparent reference to the Arthurian enchantress.
explanation.walkthrough: Lake Constance (the Bodensee) borders Germany, Switzerland and Austria; Constance is also a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Constance is a woman's given name that also names a large Alpine lake, so a lady of the lake.

clue.text: Say what you can get from taxi — a mile per gallon

indicators.note: asking what you can get from these letters invites rearranging them into something new

explanation.surface: A remark about a taxi's fuel economy in miles per gallon.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram's letters are TAXI, A, MILE, PER and G for gallon.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempli gratia, abbreviated e.g., is Latin for for example, which is what say means before an instance.

clue.text: Eliminate boring conversation of painter?

parts.note: the prefix de- means remove or eliminate, as in de-ice
gas is idle, empty talk

explanation.surface: A plea to get rid of a dull talker's chatter, apparently about an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: To de-gas would be to eliminate the gas, or boring chatter; Edgar Degas was the French painter of ballet dancers.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Degas was a French Impressionist painter, so a painter.

clue.text: Such is quick to conceal creaming off of cream by coward

definitions.text: Such is quick to conceal creaming off of cream by coward

parts.words: Such is quick to conceal creaming off of cream by coward
parts.note: the phrase after such is repeats a hard c or k sound at the start of almost every word, so it describes itself

explanation.surface: A tongue-twister about a coward skimming cream and hiding it.
explanation.walkthrough: Quick, conceal, creaming, cream and coward all begin with the same sound, so the clue is an example of its own answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alliterative describes words that repeat the same initial sound, as the clue's phrase does.

clue.text: Try to impress with fine place for 27?

explanation.surface: Showing off, or a good seat for a spectator.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 is the spectator answer to 27-across, someone who watches, and a grandstand is the main stand of seating at a sports ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To grandstand is to show off for an audience; a grandstand is the main seating for spectators.

clue.text: Quiet town on Lake Garda, peg for solvers and sleuth

parts.note: p is piano, the musical direction for quiet
Riva del Garda is a town at the north end of Lake Garda in Italy
a tee is the peg a golf ball sits on
ye is an old word for you, the solvers being addressed

explanation.surface: A detective appears among a quiet Italian lakeside town, a golf peg and the readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For solvers' means for you, the people solving, and ye is the old form of you.
explanation.definitionFit: A private eye is a private detective, so a sleuth.

clue.text: Military units have not done well

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, a British army corps
RE is the Royal Engineers, another British army corps

explanation.surface: Army regiments are criticised for a poor performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not done well' looks like a criticism but means undercooked, as rare steak is.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare meat is lightly cooked, so not well done.

clue.text: Had been, say, very well done

explanation.surface: A remark on a past achievement, praised as excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had been' is an example of the pluperfect tense; plu- read as more gives more than perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: The pluperfect is the past perfect tense, as in had been; split, it suggests more than perfect.

clue.text: Dickensian resurrectionist working with numbers?

explanation.surface: A Dickens body-snatcher is asked about his arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: Jerry Cruncher in A Tale of Two Cities digs up corpses by night; a resurrectionist was a body-snatcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry Cruncher is Dickens's grave robber, and a number cruncher is someone who does calculations.

clue.text: Always a loss?

parts.note: a loss every time is split as never a profit, then read as a firm vow not to repeat something

explanation.surface: A gloomy verdict on a venture that never pays.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as never a gain, the answer means always a loss; as a phrase it is a vow not to repeat something.
explanation.definitionFit: Split as never a gain, the phrase means there is never any profit, so always a loss.

clue.text: It hasn't been bleached, a doubtful cure

indicators.note: something doubtful is uncertain, so its letters are not fixed in place

explanation.surface: A remedy of uncertain worth, described as unbleached.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is the pale beige colour of unbleached linen or silk.

clue.text: Incomplete contrivance by setter based on 10

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me

indicators.note: incomplete means the word lacks its final letter

parts.note: a trick is a contrivance or ruse

explanation.surface: The setter owns up to an unfinished ploy involving 10.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incomplete' drops the K from TRICK; 'by' puts the setter beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The metric system is built on powers of ten, so it is based on 10.

clue.text: See 3
Best fruit for 3 1 5

explanation.surface: The finest fruit for a nursery-rhyme boy.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme Little Jack Horner put in his thumb and pulled out a plum.
explanation.definitionFit: A plum job is the best one, and the plum is the fruit Jack Horner pulled from his pie.

clue.text: Male peon, say?

parts.note: spoken, male sounds like him and peon like paean, a song of praise, so the clue is a sound-alike pair

explanation.surface: A remark about a male labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: A peon is a labourer, but said aloud it matches paean, a song of praise; HYMN sounds like him, a male.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a song of praise, which is what a paean is, and the word sounds like him, a male.

clue.text: Character getting drink at pub

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer
PH is the abbreviation for public house, a pub, as on maps

explanation.surface: Someone colourful getting a pint at the local.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a written character.

clue.text: Improvement near end of game by side?

parts.note: late means near the end, as in late in the match
a rally is a recovery or improvement

explanation.surface: A team's comeback near the final whistle, put down to one side.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are read in reverse clue order: the late part comes first, then the rally.
explanation.definitionFit: Laterally means sideways, by the side.

clue.text: Dismal conclusion to lady holding back

indicators.note: holding means one piece wraps around another
the conclusion to a word is its final part, here the last two letters

parts.note: rear means back

explanation.surface: A gloomy ending for a woman holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conclusion to' takes the last two letters of 'lady', which 'holding' puts round the word for back.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary and dismal are synonyms, both meaning gloomy and depressing.

clue.text: Jeweller formerly on guard?

explanation.surface: An old jewellery trade linked to keeping watch.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as watch man, it is someone who once sold watches; whole, it is a night guard.
explanation.definitionFit: A watchman keeps guard, and read as watch-man an old jeweller who dealt in watches.
